title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction: §21 closes Problem III, which extremizes ∫X(x)ds for a space curve with y'=p, z'=q and s=√(1+p²+q²). The first integrals Xp/s=a and Xq/s=na give z=ny+c, so the extremal is a plane curve, with dy = a dx/√(X²−m²a²) where m=n²+1. Euler then names two classical cases. For X=x the weight is the height and the curve is the catenary, read as the curve whose centre of gravity is lowest among isoperimetric curves. For X=1/√x one gets dy = a√x dx/√(1−m²a²x), the cycloid, read as the brachistochrone, since ∫ds/√x is a fall time. Problem IV: extremize ∫√(x²+y²+z²)·ds = ∫ r ds in space. With v=r and V=vs, Euler computes the partial derivatives: M=∂V/∂x=sx/v, N=sy/v, N'=sz/v, P=vp/s, P'=vq/s. He uses the general system from earlier in the memoir. Two equations are Euler–Lagrange equations: N dx = dP and N' dx = dP'. The third is M dx = dS with S = V−Pp−P'q, a Beltrami/Hamiltonian-type identity; it holds identically along solutions because dS = M dx + (N dx−dP)p + (N' dx−dP')q. Here S = v(s²−p²−q²)/s = v/s, giving: (I) sx dx/v = d(v/s); (II) sy dx/v = d(vp/s); (III) sz dx/v = d(vq/s). On the following pages Euler eliminates the variables to reach z−qx = n(y−px), which forces the curve into a plane through the origin. That relation is a ratio of angular-momentum components, i.e. it reflects rotational invariance. In modern terms ∫ r ds is the length in the conformal metric r²|dx|². With ρ=r²/2 the plane metric becomes dρ² + (2ρ)²dθ², a flat cone, so the extremals are r²cos(2θ−α) = const: rectangular hyperbolas centred at O, or lines through O.
errors: The printed/transcribed value M = sx/p should be M = sx/v. This follows from ∂(vs)/∂x = s·x/v, and equation I itself uses sx dx/v, so it is a misprint or misreading only.

No mathematical error on this page. The catenary remark is loose: the unconstrained extremal of ∫x ds is a catenary, and the 'lowest centre of gravity among isoperimetric curves' reading needs the length constraint (X = x+const), which only shifts the constant. Since the next page writes d(v/s) = sx dx/(−v), it should be checked against equation I here, which has the positive sign.

ideas.what: Extremals of ∫X(x)ds in space are planar, and reduce to the planar problem
ideas.modern_name: Reduction by cyclic coordinates / conserved momenta
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi (1744) treats the planar ∫X ds cases; this 3D version is in E740

ideas.what: X=x gives the catenary, X=1/√x gives the brachistochrone (cycloid)
ideas.modern_name: Catenary and brachistochrone as weighted-length (Jacobi metric) geodesics
ideas.usually_credited_to: Johann and Jakob Bernoulli, Leibniz, Huygens; Euler E65

ideas.what: Third equation M dx = d(V − Pp − P'q) alongside the two Euler–Lagrange equations
ideas.modern_name: Beltrami identity / energy (Hamiltonian) relation for a non-autonomous variable
ideas.where_published: E65 and earlier sections of E740

ideas.modern_name: Geodesics of the conformal metric r²|dx|² (Jacobi metric of a repulsive harmonic potential at zero energy); rectangular hyperbolas
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler for planar ∫r^n ds (sinusoidal-spiral-type curves); duality via the conformal map w=z² credited to Bohlin, Arnold
ideas.where_published: Planar central-weight cases appear in E65 (unsure of exact location); the 3D version in E740

missed.claim: Euler's laborious Cartesian elimination (next page: 'plurimam solertiam atque insignia calculi artificia') yields z−qx = n(y−px), a ratio of angular-momentum components. This is the first integral that rotational symmetry guarantees, but it is extracted ad hoc rather than recognised as a symmetry consequence. This is a minor historical pre-echo of Noether-type reasoning, well documented in the general history of conservation laws, so it is not novel.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of pedagogical/historical interest: an example of symmetry integrals obtained by brute elimination.

deep.surprise_reason: Standard variational computations. Both the catenary/brachistochrone remark and the ∫r ds problem have classical, known solutions, and Euler's methods here appear in E65. Nothing appears absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: M = sx/v (transcription and possibly print show sx/p)
In §21 the second radical should read √(1−mmaax), consistent with the first
